newsitem.title: UGANDA: Researchers agree proposal to tackle coffee plague.
newsitem.headline: Researchers agree proposal to tackle coffee plague.

text.p: Global coffee researchers meeting in the Ugandan capital Kampala have hammered out a project proposal to control and prevent the spread of coffee wilt disease in east and central Africa, officials said on Thursday.
The researchers, who met for three days with representatives of African coffee-producing nations estimate a $12.1 million, five year package is needed to fight the tracheomycosis disease.
The disease has struck Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and experts fear it could spread.
Minutes obtained from the meeting which ended on Wednesday showed the first phase of the project will last two years and is due to start on September 1. The second phase will take three years.
Details of which countries pay what have not been finalised.
Covering disease control, extension and research and development, the project will focus on Uganda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast and Rwanda.
Member countries hope to raise 50 percent of the cost from the European Union's Stabex funds, with the rest provided by the Common Fund for Commodities (CFC).

Overseen by the International Coffee Organization (ICO), the project will conduct an epidemiological survey of the environment and cultural practices, as well as attempting to breed disease-resistant varities. It will also include an implementation and extension programme to improve agricultural husbandry.
ICO official Julia Elena Serpa told Reuters her organisation will support the project's bid for funding from the CFC.
"ICO is in support of a regional approach in fighting and eradicating the disease," said Serpa at the opening of the workshop.

Ugandan scientists say tracheomycosis affects 12 of the country's coffee growing districts, 44 percent of the total, in varying intensity. They estimated the cost of containing the disease at five to seven million dollars.
So far the industry's top policy body, the Uganda Coffee Development Authority (UCDA) has spent $200,000 fighting the disease.
High rainfall in Uganda and moving plant cuttings from one area to another is said to explain the wilt's spread.
A researcher from Ivory Coast, where the disease has been brought under control, said Ugandans can only eradicate tracheomycosis if they can uproot and burn all affected plants.
"It's what we did in the 1950s when we experienced a similar problem," said the official.

The wilt threatens the lifeblood of Uganda's economy. Coffee brings in 65 percent of the country's foreign exchange earnings and employs over 2.5 million of Uganda's 20 million people in growing, processing and marketing. --Nairobi newsroom ++254 2 224-717
